title: the Samkhya Karika)
hook: the ankle bells go quiet and the dancer leaves the stage: Samkhya's picture of the world's show

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika gave us two travelers: prakriti, who moves but can't see, carrying purusha, who sees but can't move. What did your body do for you without being asked? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

The last rhythm of a classical dance recital. The drummer's hands slow. The dancer strikes her final pose, ankle bells ringing, then still. For a moment nobody in the hall moves. Then she bows, and walks off the stage. She doesn't come back out to do it all again for the same people. The dance was for them, it was seen, and it's finished. The Samkhya Karika reaches for exactly this scene near its end, when it tries to say what happens once the world has done what it came to do.
screen: `THE FINAL POSE.` → `SHE BOWS AND WALKS OFF.` → `SEEN, AND FINISHED.`

segments.voice: The verse goes like this, in paraphrase. As a dancer stops dancing once she has shown herself to the audience, so prakriti stops, once she has shown herself to purusha. Hold yesterday's travelers in mind. Prakriti carried the seer through the forest so that purusha could see. The whole unfolding, everything we counted, has been a performance with one audience in view. The Karika adds two more touches. First, prakriti is generous. She serves purusha in many ways, the text says, and asks nothing back. Purusha does nothing in return; it can't. It only watches. Second, prakriti is modest. The Karika says nothing is more modest than she is. Once she knows she has been truly seen, she doesn't show herself to that seer again. And a few verses later the text gives the last exchange, almost like a play. One says, I have seen her, and loses interest. The other says, I have been seen, and stops. That's Samkhya's picture of freedom, and notice what it isn't. It isn't fighting the world, or escaping it, or hating it. It's seeing it so completely that its hold just ends, the way a song you've finally understood stops replaying in your head. The dance isn't wasted. It was the whole point, right up until the bow. Tomorrow, on the last day of Samkhya, we hear what the seer is left with.
screen: `THE DANCER STOPS WHEN SEEN.` · `PRAKRITI IS GENEROUS.` · `PRAKRITI IS MODEST.` · `I HAVE SEEN HER. I HAVE BEEN SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch one thing all the way to its bow. Settle, and let your breath slow. Pick one sound, a breath, a hum in the room, a car going by, and stay with it from its first edge to its last. Don't grab the next one yet. Let it finish completely. Then wait, quiet, until something else steps onto the stage, and watch that one through to the end too. If you pray, you can offer each ending as it comes. The bell holds the time.
The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of freedom: prakriti as a dancer who, once truly seen, finishes her dance and leaves the stage.
Your line: the Samkhya Karika. Today, let one thing finish before you move on: a song, a cup of tea, someone's sentence. Watch it all the way to its bow. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: The dancer image from the Samkhya Karika is taught in Samkhya and Yoga study as a picture of liberation through discernment.

myth: in Samkhya, freedom means fighting the world until you escape it
the Karika's picture is seeing: once prakriti is truly seen, her dance ends.
she serves purusha in many ways and asks nothing back.
purusha repays prakriti for the dance

fork.setup: you're the dancer. the last pose is held, and you know the audience has truly seen the whole dance. what now?
options: an encore, the same dance again.
bow, and walk off the stage.
fork.reveal: the Karika says prakriti, like a dancer who has shown herself, stops. once she knows she's been seen, she doesn't appear to that seer again.

original.note: Sanskrit: a dancer; the Samkhya Karika's picture for prakriti, who stops once she has been seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty simile about a dancer.
what it means: Samkhya's whole idea of freedom: the world, once completely seen by the witness, stops binding it.
what a scholar hears: Samkhya Karika 59–61 on the dancer, her generosity and her modesty, and verse 66's closing exchange, 'I have seen' and 'I have been seen'.

notes: Paraphrases of Karika 59 (the dancer), 60 (prakriti as helpful/generous, purusha giving nothing back), 61 (nothing more modest than prakriti; once seen she does not show herself again) and 66 (the spectator and the seen). The 'I have seen her / I have been seen' lines are in the voice without quotation marks as a paraphrase. Confirm verse numbers and wording.
Original 'नर्तकी' (dancer, feminine): the Karika's verse uses 'nartakī'. Confirm.
